name: Authority Bias
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: When Credentials Substitute for Evidence
lesson.summary: Explains why borrowing trust from famous or credentialed people distorts how we judge quantum computing claims, and why expertise in one field doesn't transfer to another.
lesson.body:
You already know that a cognitive bias is a systematic shortcut your brain takes instead of doing the harder work of evaluating evidence directly. Authority bias is one of the most powerful of these shortcuts: it's the tendency to judge a claim as more likely true simply because someone impressive, credentialed, or powerful said it, rather than because the claim itself holds up under scrutiny. Your brain treats status as a proxy for accuracy, because in everyday life that proxy usually saves time and rarely costs much. A doctor's advice about your cough is probably more reliable than a stranger's, so deferring to credentials is often a reasonable heuristic. The problem is that this heuristic doesn't check whether the person's expertise actually covers the specific question being asked.

Quantum computing is an unusually good environment for this bias to misfire, because it sits at the intersection of several very different specialties: the physics of qubits, the engineering of error correction and control systems, the computer science of algorithms, and the economics of when (or whether) any of this becomes commercially useful. A person can be a genuine world-class expert in one of these layers while having no special insight into another. Someone who won major recognition for foundational work in condensed matter physics has real authority over questions about material properties or superconductivity. That same authority does not automatically extend to predicting how many years away a fault-tolerant machine is, or whether a particular company's roadmap is financially realistic ,  those are engineering and business questions, not physics questions. Your brain, however, doesn't naturally slice a person's credibility into narrow domains; it tends to apply a single global "impressive person" tag and let that tag color everything they say.

Consider a hypothetical scenario: a well-known physicist gives a public talk and casually predicts that practical quantum computers will transform an entire industry within a short timeframe. The claim gets repeated in headlines and social media, gaining momentum not because anyone checked the underlying assumptions about error rates, qubit counts, or engineering timelines, but because the source is prestigious. If you asked the same question to a systems engineer working on the actual hardware, you might get a far more cautious answer, grounded in the specific bottlenecks that field currently faces. The prediction didn't become more accurate by coming from a famous physicist; it just became more persuasive.

This is why authority bias is worth flagging separately from motivated reasoning or hype in general: it works even when the authority figure is being completely sincere and even when they have no financial stake in the outcome. The distortion happens entirely on the listener's side, in how much weight gets assigned based on the source rather than the argument. Guarding against it doesn't mean dismissing experts ,  it means asking a narrower question every time you hear a confident claim: is this person's authority actually about this specific sub-question, or just about the field in general? That single habit of re-scoping expertise is often enough to catch the bias before it shapes your judgment.
